prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock, from the magic-wavelength concept to clocks of 10^-18 accuracy

statement.case_for: I opened with twisted bilayer graphene first and optical lattice clocks sixth, but the discussion has moved me. Seven of eight members ranked B010, four of them in their top three, and the scientific case holds up under the questions I normally ask. The result is quantitative and has been reproduced independently at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and NPL, and the clocks are compared across continents at the 1e-18 level. Theory explains the systematic shifts (magic wavelengths, blackbody and higher-order light shifts), so calculation and measurement agree, which I value. The magic-wavelength idea removed a real trade-off between atom number and Doppler, recoil and collision shifts. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori made the concept and first demonstrations, and Ye's group took it to record accuracy and many-body regimes, and every proposer names the same two people. The prize would honour a lasting new capability: relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and the redefinition of the second. A condensed-matter member can still support it, because it rests on a verified physical discovery and has real use.
statement.case_against: My main reservation is that B010 is a measurement-capability prize more than a discovery of a new state or phenomenon, and it sits close to the 2005 comb prize (Hall, Hansch) and the 2012 ion-trap prize (Wineland, Haroche). A committee that wants a discovery in nature could find it incremental. The redefinition of the second is still pending, and credit for Hollberg, Takamoto, Lemonde and the ion-clock groups is outside the two names. I also worry that I am voting for the broad consensus candidate while my own scientific preference, the moire work, is less settled. If the committee leans toward a materials discovery, B051 is the better case.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first as a new measurement capability that extended time and frequency metrology by orders of magnitude, with a clean two-person credit and independent confirmation at several national labs.
responses.response: I agree on the reproducibility and the two-name attribution, and this moved my ranking up from sixth. I do not fully accept the premise that a measurement capability counts the same as a discovery. The 1e-18 level is what makes it a physics result, since it opens relativistic time dilation over millimetre scales and constant-variation tests. I would want the citation to name that physics and not only the instrument.

responses.point: Lindroth values the idea of Katori's magic wavelength made quantitative through accurate atomic-structure theory, with Ye's group delivering the 1e-18 clocks and many-body work, and notes the redefinition of the second is approaching.
responses.response: Your point that the systematic shifts are controlled by calculable atomic theory is what persuades me, because it is the theory-to-measurement link I look for in materials. I would press one qualification. The redefinition of the second is a CIPM process and should not drive the timing of a physics prize. The case must stand on the science, and it does. Could you say whether the blackbody-shift uncertainty is now settled enough that the 1e-18 claim is independently secure?

responses.point: Mehlig ranks topological insulators first as a universal mechanism beyond the Landau paradigm, but notes the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal is outside the credited names and that Hasan's 3D work is also decisive, so a three-person set is awkward.
responses.response: I ranked B047 second and agree on the science, but I think your attribution objection is serious and is why I will not lead with it. Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is the cleanest set I can build from the supplied names, yet it omits BHZ and the 3D ARPES branch. The field also received the 2016 prize for topological phases, so the argument for urgency is weaker than for something not yet recognised. I keep it as an alternative, not as my preferred configuration.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron microscopy first: it broke the Scherzer limit, gave routine sub-angstrom imaging, has a compact Rose-Haider-Urban credit, and recognition is arguably overdue.
responses.response: I ranked B039 seventh, and I do not dispute its impact on my own field, since atomic-resolution spectroscopy is essential to materials theory. The credit is clean. My reservation is the same as for B010 turned the other way: it is an instrument prize with a weaker physics-discovery element. If the committee wants an enabling-tool prize, the optical lattice clock has stronger fundamental-physics consequences than a microscope. Krivanek's STEM corrector being outside the credit also troubles me.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first as an instrument-driven discovery that opened neutrino astronomy, with Halzen, Karle and Spiering as leaders, while admitting that the size of the collaboration makes the three-person limit a fairness problem.
responses.response: I defer to you and Danielsson on astroparticle physics, which is far from my own. The diffuse flux is secure and the opening of a new window is a real discovery. My worry is the one you raise: with a large collaboration, a three-name prize risks being contested, and source identification remains thin. B061 had only three members rank it at all, so I do not see it winning a broad majority, but I would not object if the committee leans that way.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers a precision-measurement prize so soon after the 2005 (Hall, Hansch) and 2012 (Wineland, Haroche) prizes in neighbouring areas.
Whether the 1e-18 accuracy claims for strontium lattice clocks are fully independent of blackbody-shift and lattice-light-shift systematics.
Whether Hollberg, Takamoto or ion-clock contributors deserve credit that a two-person prize omits.
For B051, whether the superconducting pairing mechanism in twisted bilayer graphene needs to be understood before the committee proceeds, and how to weigh Yuan Cao's first-author role.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B010. For the moire candidate B051, MacDonald and I are in the same electronic-structure theory community and may have co-authors or collaborators in common, but I have no direct link I can identify. My Uppsala and Los Alamos ties do not touch Katori or Ye.
